_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 2 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 4 Objects and Plans. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (objects; a plan for each object; build one and test one; repeats for objects too; which object is it; real programs), in the lesson's own words and with the lesson's own cat, dog, tree and ball. Every sprite move on screen is the LESSON'S arithmetic, taken from ART.run - move right is one square capped at three, grow is times 1.4 capped at 2.2, repeat 3 times unrolls to three moves - so the film and the lesson cannot disagree about what a block does.
title: Objects and Plans
subtitle: Grade 2 Computing
objectives: Know how to plan the instructions for objects within programs.
Know how to recreate algorithms as programs.
Identify the benefits of regularly testing programs throughout their development.
Understand that programs instruct computers how to run algorithms.

beats.say: A cat and a dog, on one stage. Two objects, and two different plans.
Each object needs its own blocks. Plan each one before you build it.
A program can have more than one thing inside it.
A cat, a dog, a ball. Each one is called an object.
An object is a thing that can be given its own instructions.
The cat's blocks move the cat. The dog's blocks move the dog.
Blocks make a program. A program tells the computer how to run an algorithm.
Before you build, plan. What should each object do?
The cat walks to the tree, then says hello. That is its plan.
The dog jumps twice, then spins. That is a different plan.
The dog is a different object, so it gets different blocks.
What should the tree do? Nothing. It gets no blocks at all.
Now build. Turn each plan into blocks, one object at a time.
Build the cat's program first: move right, move right, say hello.
Run it. Did the cat do its plan? Yes it did. That was a test.

at.did: Did the cat do its plan?

beats.say: Now build the dog's program: jump, jump, spin. Run that one too.
Test each program as you build it. Then every bug stays small.
An object's plan can use the repeat block, like any other program.
The dog must move left three times. That is three move left blocks.
Or use repeat 3 times, then move left. That is only two blocks.
Same moves, fewer blocks. The repeat block always goes first.
A stage can hold several objects at the same time.
Each one carries its own blocks, and they all run side by side.
So when something goes wrong, ask which object is doing it.
Check that object's blocks. Leave the other objects alone.
Real programs have lots of objects, each with its own plan.
A game has a player and enemies. Each one is an object.
An animation has several characters. They all run at the same time.
A traffic light has three lights: red, amber and green.
Each light is an object with its own plan for when to be on.
Every object in a program gets its own plan and its own blocks.
Plan it, build the program, then run it and test it.
On one stage, every object quietly does its own job.
